Tutorial 3 of 6

Next.js Essentials

Next.js is a framework built on React. You still write React components, and Next adds the parts React leaves out: routing, a server, data fetching, caching and deployment. Examples use Next 16.4 with the App Router, TypeScript and Cache Components, which is how create-next-app sets up a new project today.

Create the app

The defaults give you TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, a linter and the App Router. The structure:

The generated next.config.ts also switches on Cache Components (cacheComponents: true). It changes how pages are rendered and cached, and every example on this page is written for it: Next builds as much of each page as it can ahead of time, and anything that depends on the request must be marked. Data fetching and caching explains the rule.

Concept: a Next app runs in two places. Some code runs on the server, some in the browser. Most of this tutorial is about knowing which is which.

Pages and routes

Folders inside app/ are URL segments. A folder becomes a page when it contains page.tsx. There is no router config.

FileURL
app/page.tsx/
app/about/page.tsx/about
app/users/[id]/page.tsx/users/42, /users/7
app/(shop)/cart/page.tsx/cart (parentheses group folders without changing the URL)

The id is only known when a request arrives, so the part that reads it sits inside <Suspense>. Next prerenders everything outside the boundary, sends the fallback first, and streams the real content in. Await params directly in the page function with no boundary and npm run build fails with "uncached or runtime data during prerendering".

Shortcut: a loading.tsx file next to the page wraps the whole page in a Suspense boundary for you (next chapter). Then the page itself may be async and await params at the top.

Layouts and special files

A layout.tsx wraps every page in its folder and below. It stays mounted while you navigate, so the nav does not re-render.

Next looks for a few file names in each route folder and wires them up for you:

FileShown when
loading.tsxThe page is still waiting for data. It becomes the Suspense fallback for the whole page.
error.tsxThe page threw an error (must start with "use client")
not-found.tsxYou call notFound() or no route matches

Navigation

Link navigates without a full reload and preloads the target page when the link scrolls into view.

Server and client components

This is the main idea of Next. Every component is a server component by default. It runs only on the server, and its code never reaches the browser. Add "use client" at the top of a file when the component needs the browser.

NeedServer componentClient component
Read the database, use secretsYesNo
async / await in the componentYesNo
useState, useEffectNoYes
onClick, onChangeNoYes
Adds JavaScript to the browser bundleNoYes

The usual pattern: a server component fetches the data and passes it to a small client component for the interactive part. Below, page.tsx is a server component and LikeButton.tsx is a client component. The fetch lives in its own component inside <Suspense>, so the heading is prerendered and the list streams in.

Rule of thumb: start on the server. Move to the client only the smallest piece that needs state or clicks.

Data fetching and caching

In a server component you just await. No useEffect, no loading state in your own code, and the user receives finished HTML.

With Cache Components, Next tries to prerender every page at build time. Data it cannot know in advance has to be put in one of two boxes, and the build refuses a page that does neither:

The data isYou writeResult
Fresh for every request, or personal: a fetch, a database read, cookies(), headers(), params, searchParamsRead it in a component wrapped in <Suspense>The page shell is prerendered, the fallback shows first, the data streams in
The same for everyone and fine to reuse for a while"use cache" in the function or component, with cacheLifeThe result is stored and becomes part of the prerendered page

Fresh data: stream it

The heading is static. Stats runs on each request and replaces the fallback when it is ready.

Shared data: cache it

Arguments of a cached function are part of the cache key, so getUser(7) and getUser(8) are stored separately. cacheLife takes a profile name: "seconds", "minutes", "hours", "days", "weeks" or "max". To throw a cached result away after a change, see Server Actions.

If you forget

Older tutorials cache per request with fetch(url, { cache: "force-cache" }) or { next: { revalidate: 60 } }, and await data at the top of an async page. That is the model before Cache Components. It still works in a project with cacheComponents off, but it is not what a new app uses.

Need two things at once? Start both, then await together: const [user, posts] = await Promise.all([getUser(), getPosts()]);

Server Actions: forms and mutations

A Server Action is a function marked "use server". You pass it to a form, and Next calls it on the server when the form submits. No API endpoint and no fetch to write.

After a change, cached data is out of date. Tag it where it is read, with cacheTag("todos") inside the "use cache" function, and expire the tag where it is changed:

CallEffectUse it
updateTag("todos")Expires the tag at once, so the user sees their own change. Server Actions only.After a form submit
revalidateTag("todos", "max")Serves the old result while a fresh one is prepared in the backgroundWebhooks, content updates where a short delay is fine
revalidatePath("/todos")Invalidates everything cached for one URLWhen you do not know the tags

Important: a Server Action is a public endpoint under the hood. Validate the input and check the user inside every action.

Route handlers: API endpoints

A route.ts file is an HTTP endpoint. Export a function per method.

A GET handler follows the same rule as a page: one that returns fixed data, like this, can be prerendered, and one that reads the request, cookies or a database runs on each request. Other methods always run on request.

Use route handlers for things called from outside your UI: webhooks, mobile apps, other services. For your own pages, server components and Server Actions are simpler.

Auth

The pattern: a Server Action logs in and stores the token in an httpOnly cookie (JavaScript in the browser cannot read it). A proxy file blocks protected URLs before they render. Server code reads the cookie when it needs the user.

2. Block protected routes

The file sits in the project root, next to app/. Before Next 16 it was called middleware.ts and the function middleware. Same idea.

3. Use the session on the server

Reading a cookie is request data, so Welcome sits inside <Suspense>, as in Data fetching.

Important: the proxy is a fast first check, not the only one. Check the session again where the data is read, as the component above does.

For Google or GitHub login, password reset and session rotation, use a library instead of writing it yourself: Auth.js, Better Auth or Clerk.

Styling, images and fonts

Tailwind is already set up by create-next-app. CSS Modules also work with no setup.

Image resizes the file, serves a modern format, lazy loads it, and reserves space so the page does not jump. Put the file in public/.

next/font downloads the font at build time and serves it from your own domain. No request to Google from the browser, no flash of the wrong font.

Metadata and SEO

Export metadata from a page or layout. Next writes the <title> and meta tags into the server HTML, so search engines and link previews see them.

For a title that depends on the URL, export generateMetadata. It receives the same params as the page.

Same rule as pages: metadata that reads params, cookies or uncached data is resolved at request time. That is fine here because the page body already streams. On a page that is otherwise fully static, Next asks you to cache that data with "use cache" instead.

Environment variables

Read them with process.env.API_URL. Only names starting with NEXT_PUBLIC_ are sent to the browser. Everything else stays on the server, so secrets are safe in server components, actions and route handlers.

From Figma to pages

The mapping is the same as in React, with a Next home for each piece:

In FigmaIn Next
Variables (colors, spacing)@theme block in app/globals.css
Component and variantsFile in components/, variants as props
Frame (a screen)app/<route>/page.tsx
Shared header, sidebarlayout.tsx
Imagespublic/ + next/image
Text styles and fontsnext/font

With an AI agent (Figma MCP)

Tell the agent which parts are interactive. Only those become client components. The rest stays on the server.

How pages get rendered

Next decides per route, and often per part of a page, from what the code uses. A page is a prerendered shell plus optional holes that are filled at request time.

Part of a pageHTML is builtTriggered byGood for
StaticOnce, at build timeNo data, or only data known at buildMarketing pages, docs, headings and layout
CachedAt build, then refreshed by cacheLife or when its tag is expired"use cache"Product lists, blogs, pricing
StreamedOn every request, inside a <Suspense> boundarycookies(), headers(), params, searchParams, uncached fetchesDashboards, anything per user

npm run build prints what each route became. This is the table for the examples on this page, built together:

  • /pricing is static with a lifetime: that is cacheLife("hours") from the cached example.
  • /dashboard, /products and /users/[id] are partial: a static shell with a streamed hole.
  • /api/health is dynamic because the file also has a POST handler.

For dynamic segments you can prebuild known pages with generateStaticParams.

Build and deploy

Unlike a plain React build, this is a running Node server, not a folder of static files. Three common ways to host it:

  • Vercel: connect the Git repo and push. Zero config.
  • Docker or Kubernetes: set output: "standalone" in next.config.ts, copy .next/standalone into the image, run node server.js.
  • Static only: set output: "export" to get plain files, but you lose server features (actions, cookies, dynamic rendering).

The mental model

  • Folders are routes. Special file names (page, layout, loading, error) are roles.
  • Components run on the server unless you say "use client".
  • Read data by awaiting in server components. Change data with Server Actions.
  • Secrets and cookies live on the server. The browser gets HTML and only the JavaScript it needs.
  • Request data goes inside <Suspense> and streams. Shared data is cached with "use cache". The build tells you when a page does neither.
